questions.stem: The biopsychosocial approach to psychological disorder proposes that disorders are best understood as:
options: the result of faulty thinking patterns that a person has learnt in childhood
the result of a person's relationships, with little role for biological factors
the result of interacting biological, psychological and social factors
the result of a chemical imbalance in the brain that medication can correct
questions.explanation: The biopsychosocial approach holds that biological, psychological and social factors all contribute, and interact, in the development of a disorder and in recovery. Explanations based only on brain chemistry or only on thinking are single-factor approaches that it was designed to move beyond.

questions.stem: Which is a biological risk factor for psychological disorder?
options: Rumination
Disorganised attachment
Loss of a significant relationship
Substance use
questions.explanation: Biological risk factors include genes, medication, sleep and substance use, which act on the body and brain. Rumination is a psychological factor, and disorganised attachment and relationships are social factors.

questions.stem: Rumination, a psychological risk factor for disorder, refers to:
options: having an insecure early bond with a parent or other caregiver
using alcohol or other drugs to escape from unpleasant feelings
repeatedly and passively dwelling on negative thoughts and feelings
deliberately avoiding any situation that might cause anxiety or fear
questions.explanation: Rumination is repetitive, passive focus on distress and its causes and consequences without moving towards solutions; it is linked to depression and anxiety. Avoidance is a behaviour, and insecure early bonds describe attachment, a social factor.

questions.stem: Which is a psychological risk factor for psychological disorder?
options: Loss of a close friendship
Impaired reasoning and memory
Inherited genetic vulnerability
Side effects of prescribed medication
questions.explanation: The syllabus lists rumination, impaired reasoning and memory, and stress as psychological risk factors, because they involve mental processes. Genes and medication are biological factors, and the loss of a significant relationship is a social factor.

questions.stem: Which correctly classifies these risk factors: a family history of anxiety; ongoing stress at work; a recent relationship breakdown?
options: Psychological; biological; social
Social; psychological; biological
Biological; psychological; social
Biological; social; psychological
questions.explanation: A family history points to genetic vulnerability, a biological factor; stress is listed as a psychological factor; and the loss of a significant relationship is a social factor. Work is a social setting, but the syllabus classes the stress itself as psychological.

questions.stem: A child whose caregiver is frightening and unpredictable may form a disorganised attachment. Why is this classed as a social risk factor for later psychological disorder?
options: It arises from the child taking medication prescribed by a doctor
It arises from the child's relationship with the people around them
It arises from genes the child inherited from the caregiver at conception
It arises from the child's own repetitive thinking about negative events
questions.explanation: Attachment is a relationship between a child and caregiver, so problems in it are social factors. A genetic vulnerability passed on by a parent would be biological, and repetitive negative thinking is rumination, a psychological factor.

questions.stem: Lucy has been sleeping only four or five hours a night for several months while studying and working. How might this act as a risk factor for psychological disorder?
options: Ongoing sleep loss impairs mood and emotional regulation, a biological risk
Ongoing sleep loss is a social risk because it reduces time with friends only
Ongoing sleep loss is a protective factor because it increases alertness
Ongoing sleep loss affects physical health but has no effect on mental health
questions.explanation: Sleep is listed as a biological risk factor: persistent sleep loss affects brain function, raising irritability, low mood and anxiety and reducing the ability to cope. It does not increase alertness; it reduces it.

questions.stem: Two brothers share a genetic vulnerability to anxiety. One develops generalised anxiety disorder after years of high stress and a habit of rumination; the other, with supportive friends and low stress, does not. What does this best illustrate?
options: Biological, psychological and social factors interact to produce disorder
Genes alone determine whether a person will develop a psychological disorder
Psychological factors alone determine whether a person will develop a disorder
Social factors have no influence once a person has a genetic vulnerability
questions.explanation: The same genetic vulnerability led to different outcomes depending on psychological factors (stress, rumination) and social factors (support), which is the core idea of the biopsychosocial approach. A genetic vulnerability raises risk but does not make a disorder inevitable.

questions.stem: Why does the biopsychosocial approach draw on evidence from psychology, psychiatry and social work?
options: Social work studies biological causes, which psychology and psychiatry ignore
Each discipline focuses on a different set of factors that contribute to disorder
Each discipline uses exactly the same methods, so their results confirm each other
Only psychiatry can diagnose disorders, so the other fields simply repeat its findings
questions.explanation: Psychiatry contributes medical and biological knowledge, psychology contributes knowledge of thinking, emotion and behaviour, and social work contributes knowledge of relationships, communities and social conditions. Together they cover all three parts of the approach.

questions.stem: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is characterised by:
options: intense fear of one particular object or situation that the person avoids
sudden episodes of intense fear that are always triggered by a specific object
persistent low mood and a loss of interest in activities once enjoyed
excessive, hard-to-control worry about many everyday matters over a long period
questions.explanation: GAD involves persistent, excessive worry about a range of events or activities, such as work, health and family, that the person finds hard to control, on more days than not for at least six months. Fear focused on one object or situation is a specific phobia.

questions.stem: Which set of symptoms most clearly suggests generalised anxiety disorder?
options: Hallucinations, delusions and disorganised speech with withdrawal from friends
Fear of dogs, a racing heart near dogs and avoiding parks where dogs are walked
Episodes of elevated mood, high energy and little need for sleep lasting days
Constant worry with restlessness, muscle tension and poor concentration
questions.explanation: GAD's worry is accompanied by physical and cognitive symptoms such as restlessness, fatigue, muscle tension, irritability, poor concentration and disturbed sleep. Fear limited to dogs points to a specific phobia, and elevated mood with high energy suggests mania.

questions.stem: Priya feels intense fear whenever she has an injection or sees blood, sometimes almost faints, and has avoided medical appointments for years. This is best described as:
options: generalised anxiety disorder
an adaptive fear response
a personality disorder
a specific phobia
questions.explanation: A specific phobia is a marked, persistent fear of a particular object or situation, here blood and injections, that is out of proportion to the danger and leads to avoidance. Her fear is focused on one type of situation rather than worry about many matters, so it is not GAD.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a specific phobia from an ordinary, adaptive fear?
options: The fear is out of proportion to the danger and causes avoidance that disrupts life
The fear is triggered by a real danger and fades once the danger has passed
The fear is felt only by people who have been physically hurt by the object
The fear is about many different situations rather than one particular object
questions.explanation: In a phobia the fear is excessive and persistent, and avoidance interferes with daily life. A fear that matches a real danger and passes is adaptive. Phobias can develop without direct harm, for example through observation, and fear about many situations describes GAD.

questions.stem: Which statement about the prevalence of anxiety disorders in Australia is accurate?
options: They are the most common group of mental disorders and occur equally in both sexes
They are rare in adults and occur almost only in children and young adolescents
They are the most common group of mental disorders and are more common in females
They are the least common group of mental disorders and are more common in males
questions.explanation: National surveys consistently find anxiety disorders are the most common group of mental disorders in Australia, ahead of affective disorders such as depression, and that they are more common among females than males.

questions.stem: After seeing his mother scream and panic whenever she saw a spider, Leo developed an intense fear of spiders without ever being bitten. Which perceived cause of phobia does this illustrate?
options: Disorganised attachment
Observational learning
Classical conditioning
Genetic vulnerability
questions.explanation: Leo acquired the fear by watching a model react, which is observational learning. Classical conditioning would require Leo himself to experience a frightening event paired with spiders, such as being bitten.

questions.stem: Mila was bitten by a dog at the age of six and now panics whenever she sees any dog, even small, friendly ones on a lead. Which perceived cause of phobia does this best illustrate?
options: Classical conditioning
Observational learning
Genetic vulnerability
Rumination
questions.explanation: The dog (a neutral stimulus) was paired with the pain and fright of the bite, so dogs became a conditioned stimulus for fear, which has generalised to all dogs. Observational learning would involve acquiring the fear by watching someone else's reaction.

questions.stem: Which explanation of generalised anxiety disorder is psychological rather than biological or social?
options: Low activity of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA in brain areas linked to fear
Growing up in a family where several relatives also have anxiety disorders
Living in an unsafe neighbourhood with little support from friends or family
A tendency to overestimate threat and believe that worrying prevents bad outcomes
questions.explanation: Beliefs that the world is threatening and that worry is useful are cognitive, psychological factors that keep the worry going. GABA activity is biological, and an unsafe neighbourhood with little support is social. A family history could be genetic or learnt, so it is not clearly psychological.

questions.stem: In relation to psychological disorder, stigma refers to:
options: the side effects that some people experience when taking prescribed medication
the improvement that occurs when a person expects a treatment to work
negative attitudes that lead people to be devalued or discriminated against
the set of criteria clinicians use to decide whether a person has a disorder
questions.explanation: Stigma is a mark of disgrace: negative stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination directed at people with a psychological disorder. Improvement due to expectation is the placebo effect.

questions.stem: Sam believes that having depression means he is weak, so he hides his symptoms and will not see a psychologist. This is an example of:
options: public stigma increasing help-seeking
the placebo effect reducing symptoms
rumination increasing help-seeking
self-stigma reducing help-seeking
questions.explanation: Self-stigma occurs when a person applies negative public stereotypes to themselves, leading to shame and secrecy that stop them seeking help. Stigma reduces help-seeking rather than increasing it.

questions.stem: A school wants more students experiencing anxiety to seek help early. Which strategy best targets stigma as a barrier to help-seeking?
options: Inviting people with lived experience of anxiety to talk openly about their recovery
Requiring students who are anxious to see the school counsellor in front of their class
Telling students that anxiety is rare, so they are unlikely to ever be affected by it
Removing information about mental health services from the school's website
questions.explanation: Contact with people who have recovered challenges stereotypes and shows that disorders are common and treatable, which reduces stigma. Public referral increases embarrassment, and saying anxiety is rare makes those affected feel more different.

questions.stem: Psychotherapy is best described as:
options: treatment of a disorder through surgery that destroys or disconnects brain tissue
treatment of a disorder through structured talking with a trained therapist
treatment of a disorder through medication that changes neurotransmitter activity
treatment of a disorder through electrical stimulation that induces a brief seizure
questions.explanation: Psychotherapies, such as cognitive behavioural therapy, use psychological techniques and the relationship with a therapist to change thoughts, emotions and behaviour. Medication that alters neurotransmitter activity is pharmacotherapy.

questions.stem: A therapist helps a client with generalised anxiety disorder to notice thoughts such as 'Something terrible is bound to happen', test the evidence for them and replace them with more realistic thoughts. This is a feature of:
options: cognitive behavioural therapy
pharmacotherapy
electroconvulsive therapy
psychosurgery
questions.explanation: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is a psychotherapy based on the idea that thoughts, feelings and behaviour are linked; it identifies and challenges unhelpful thinking and changes behaviour. It involves no medication or physical intervention.

questions.stem: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), used to treat depression and anxiety disorders, work by:
options: destroying serotonin in the synapse, so less of it reaches the receptors
inducing a brief seizure, which releases serotonin throughout the brain
blocking the reuptake of serotonin, so more remains in the synapse
blocking serotonin receptors, so serotonin has less effect on the neuron
questions.explanation: SSRIs slow the reabsorption of serotonin by the presynaptic neuron, increasing the amount available in the synapse to act on receptors. Blocking receptors would reduce serotonin's effect, the opposite of what SSRIs are intended to do.

questions.stem: Benzodiazepines quickly reduce anxiety, but they are usually prescribed only for short periods. Why?
options: They can cause dependence and tolerance with long-term use
They take several months of daily use before any effect appears
They work only when combined with electroconvulsive therapy
They permanently change the structure of the person's brain
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines enhance the calming effect of GABA and act within hours, but with regular use people can develop tolerance and dependence, with withdrawal symptoms on stopping. Medication that takes weeks to act describes SSRIs.

questions.stem: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is most often used for:
options: specific phobias that first developed in early childhood
personality disorders that have been present since adolescence
severe depression that has not responded to other treatments
mild anxiety in people who prefer not to take medication
questions.explanation: ECT is mainly used for severe or treatment-resistant depression, or when a rapid response is needed. It is not a first treatment for mild anxiety or phobias, where psychotherapy is preferred.

questions.stem: Which statement about modern electroconvulsive therapy is accurate?
options: It is given while the person is fully awake so they can report how they feel during the treatment
It permanently removes the part of the brain thought to be responsible for the person's symptoms
It is a form of talking therapy in which the person discusses distressing memories with a therapist
It is given under general anaesthetic with a muscle relaxant, and memory loss is a possible side effect
questions.explanation: In modern ECT a brief electric current is passed through the brain to induce a controlled seizure while the person is anaesthetised and given a muscle relaxant. Short-term confusion and some memory loss are recognised side effects. Removing or disconnecting brain tissue describes psychosurgery.

questions.stem: Psychosurgery is best described as:
options: surgery to repair damage to the brain after a head injury or stroke
any treatment for a disorder that is delivered in a hospital setting
a brief electrical current passed through the brain to cause a seizure
surgery that destroys or disconnects brain tissue to relieve symptoms
questions.explanation: Psychosurgery deliberately alters brain tissue to treat a psychological disorder. Historical procedures such as the lobotomy caused severe harm; modern procedures are precise and rare, used only as a last resort for severe, treatment-resistant cases.

questions.stem: Which comparison of treatments for psychological disorders is most accurate?
options: Psychotherapy builds coping skills that can last after treatment ends; medication may act faster but symptoms can return when it stops
Psychotherapy acts within hours; medication takes years to have any effect and is used only once other treatments fail
Psychotherapy is a last resort for treatment-resistant cases; psychosurgery is the usual first treatment for mild anxiety
Psychotherapy changes brain tissue permanently; ECT is a talking therapy that teaches clients new ways of thinking
questions.explanation: Psychotherapies teach skills the person keeps, which may reduce relapse, whereas medication can relieve symptoms more quickly but relapse is common if it is stopped without other treatment. Psychosurgery and ECT are reserved for severe cases, not first treatments.

questions.stem: Why are ECT and psychosurgery usually considered only after psychotherapy and medication have failed?
options: They are less effective than doing nothing for every psychological disorder
They can be given only to people who have never taken any medication
They have been banned for use in Australia for all psychological disorders
They are more invasive and carry greater risks of lasting side effects
questions.explanation: Both directly intervene in the brain, ECT through induced seizures with risks such as memory loss and psychosurgery through irreversible tissue changes, so less invasive treatments are tried first. Both remain available for severe, treatment-resistant cases.

questions.stem: Support for psychological disorders can be given to the individual, the family or the wider community. Which is an example of a community-level intervention?
options: A psychologist gives a young man with generalised anxiety disorder weekly CBT sessions
A doctor prescribes an SSRI to a woman with depression and reviews her each month
Parents attend sessions to learn how to support their teenage son with a phobia
A council funds mental health awareness training for local sports club volunteers
questions.explanation: Training sports club volunteers reaches many people in the community and can reduce stigma and encourage early help-seeking. CBT and medication are individual treatments, and sessions for parents are a family-level intervention.

questions.stem: The placebo effect is:
options: a change in results caused by the researcher's expectations of the study
an improvement that occurs because a person expects a treatment to work
an improvement that occurs because a drug's active ingredient is effective
a worsening of symptoms caused by the side effects of a real medication
questions.explanation: A placebo is an inactive treatment, such as a sugar pill; improvement after receiving it comes from expectation rather than any active ingredient. A change caused by the researcher's expectations is the experimenter effect.

questions.stem: In a drug trial for anxiety, one group receives the new drug and another receives an identical-looking pill with no active ingredient. Why is the second group included?
options: To increase the number of participants who experience side effects
To allow the researcher to know exactly who is taking the real drug
To control for improvement that comes from expecting the treatment to work
To make sure every participant receives the active drug at some point
questions.explanation: The placebo group shows how much improvement occurs from expectation alone; the drug is effective only if the drug group improves significantly more. Hiding which pill each person gets controls their expectations.

questions.stem: In a double-blind drug trial, neither the participants nor the researchers who assess them know who received the drug. What does the double-blind procedure add beyond a single-blind design?
options: It controls the placebo effect, which a single-blind design cannot control
It removes the need for a placebo group, since nobody knows the condition
It makes sure participants are randomly allocated to the two groups
It controls the experimenter effect as well as the placebo effect
questions.explanation: A single-blind design hides the condition from participants, controlling the placebo effect. Hiding it from the researchers as well stops their expectations from influencing how they treat participants or rate symptoms. Random allocation is a separate procedure.

questions.stem: In a trial, symptoms of depression fell by 40% in the drug group and by 30% in the placebo group. What is the most valid conclusion?
options: Much of the drug group's improvement could be due to expectation, not the drug
The drug is ineffective because the placebo group also showed an improvement
The drug caused all of the 40% improvement shown by the drug group
The placebo is more effective than the drug because it has no side effects
questions.explanation: The placebo group improved by 30% without any active ingredient, so expectation and other non-drug factors could account for most of the drug group's improvement; only the extra 10% may be due to the drug, if the difference is statistically significant. The drug is not shown to be ineffective, because the drug group still improved more.

questions.stem: A study reports the 12-month prevalence of generalised anxiety disorder as 4% in Country A and 2% in Country B. What does '12-month prevalence of 4%' mean?
options: 4% of people with GAD in the population recovered within the past year
4% of people treated for GAD in the past year needed a second treatment
4% of the population met the criteria for GAD at some time in the past year
4% of the population developed GAD for the first time in the past year
questions.explanation: Prevalence is the proportion of a population who have a disorder over a stated period, here any time in the past 12 months, including existing cases. New cases arising in a period are called incidence.

questions.stem: A survey using one diagnostic interview finds a much lower reported rate of depression in Country X than in Country Y. In Country X, people commonly describe distress as physical complaints such as fatigue and pain. What is the most valid interpretation?
options: The difference shows that culture has no influence on psychological disorder
The difference may partly reflect how distress is expressed, not only true rates
The difference proves that people in Country X are biologically protected from depression
The difference proves that the diagnostic interview was more reliable in Country X
questions.explanation: If distress is expressed as physical symptoms, an interview built around emotional symptoms may miss cases, so lower reported rates may partly be a measurement issue. Stigma and access to services can also affect reported prevalence, so the data cannot prove a biological difference.

questions.stem: Read this hypothetical survey data on 12-month prevalence of specific phobia. Country P: females 12%, males 5%. Country Q: females 9%, males 4%. Which conclusion is supported?
options: The female-to-male ratio was exactly the same in the two countries
In both countries the rate in females was more than twice that in males
In both countries specific phobia was more common in males than in females
Specific phobia was more common in Country Q than in Country P for both sexes
questions.explanation: In Country P, 12% against 5% is a ratio of 2.4, and in Country Q, 9% against 4% is 2.25, so in both countries females had more than twice the rate of males. The ratios differ, so they are not exactly the same, and Country P's rates were higher for both sexes.

questions.stem: Why should prevalence data from different countries be compared with caution?
options: Prevalence can only be measured in countries that use the DSM-5-TR
Countries may use different diagnostic methods, samples and definitions
Psychological disorders occur only in some countries and not in others
Prevalence data are always collected from the same people in every country
questions.explanation: Differences in diagnostic tools, survey methods, sampling, translation and cultural attitudes to reporting distress all affect the figures, so a difference in reported prevalence may not reflect a real difference in rates. Disorders are found worldwide, and countries using the ICD-11 also measure prevalence.
